paras: The attempted lynching of two Black men in Pike County, Missouri, took place shortly before September 12, 1903, when crowds sought to hang two young men charged with attempted assault on a white woman. A constable spirited the men away from the first crowd, and the sheriff and his armed family turned back a second mob at the Bowling Green jail. Missouri papers told it as a story of the constable's "nerve."
The two men, described only as "young negroes," were charged with attempted assault on a white woman; no one was named.

According to the fullest account, a "large crowd gathered to hang the culprits," but George D. May, a constable of Buffalo township, took the two men away before the crowd "had time to organize" and by ten o'clock that night had lodged them in the jail at Bowling Green.

At about the same hour a second mob arrived on a freight train, "determined to get the men." Sheriff Lindsey met the crowd at the fence and told them he would shoot the first man who came into the jail yard. His wife and two daughters stood with him, each armed with a pistol, and the mob dispersed "after considerable mutterings."
The two men were later taken to Troy for safe keeping. No report of a trial, of the men's later fate or of any arrest of mob members appears in the coverage.

The Laclede Blade ran the fullest account on September 12 in a column of Missouri news under the headline "Saved Lives of Two Negroes." It praised May's "cool nerve" and the sheriff's family, called the accused "the culprits" and passed no judgment on the mobs.

A syndicated "News Resume" column, run by the Marble Hill Press on September 16 and the Jackson Herald on September 17, cut the story to one line crediting May's "nerve in outwitting an angry mob" at Louisiana, Mo.
The accounts differ on place: the fuller Laclede Blade item names a Buffalo township constable and the Bowling Green jail, while the digest gives Louisiana, Mo.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of two Black men in Pike County, Missouri (1903)
bases: A crowd gathered to hang two young Black men accused of attempted assault, and a second mob came to the jail 'determined to get the men' before being turned back, an attempted lynching with no one killed (A1, A2).
The mobs meant to hang the two accused men without lawful authority on an accusation of attempted assault, but the constable and sheriff kept them from the crowds and no one was killed (A1, A2).

The only full account is the Missouri state-news item in A1; the one-line digest in A2 (reprinted in A3) agrees on the core event but adds no independent detail and gives a different place, so it cannot be shown to be an independent report.

accounts.label: Missouri state-news item
accounts.gist: Constable May hustled the two accused away from a crowd gathered to hang them and jailed them at Bowling Green; a second mob arrived by freight train and was turned back by Sheriff Lindsey and his armed wife and daughters, after which the men were taken to Troy.

accounts.label: News digest
accounts.gist: Constable May prevented the lynching of two negroes at Louisiana, Mo., by outwitting an angry mob.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Saved Lives of Two Negroes', the item praised the constable's 'cool nerve' and the sheriff's family's stand while calling the accused 'the culprits' and leaving the mob unnamed and unjudged.
A ready-made 'News Resume' column reduced the episode to one line crediting May's 'nerve in outwitting an angry mob'.

versions.value: Buffalo township constable; jail at Bowling Green, Pike County; later Troy

conflicts.note: A1 is the fuller account and names the jail where the second mob was turned back; the one-line digest names Louisiana, Mo., and may refer to where the first crowd gathered or be an error. The texts do not settle it.

record_check.dossier: Two unnamed young Black men ('young negroes').
Not stated; on or before 1903-09-12 (could be late August).
Jail confrontation at Bowling Green; the digest gives Louisiana, Mo.; the first crowd's location is not stated beyond the constable's Buffalo township.
Threat; the second mob was turned back at the jail fence without entering, so 'siege' overstates it.
white: 3 items in 3 papers (1903-09-12 to 1903-09-17); no Black-press coverage found.

info: Not stated; the event occurred on or before September 12, 1903, the earliest print date. The jail confrontation took place at about ten o'clock at night.
The accused were hustled away from a crowd by a constable of Buffalo township and lodged in the jail at Bowling Green, where the second mob arrived; they were later taken to Troy.
Charged with attempted assault on a white woman (unnamed).
A 'large crowd' that gathered to hang the men, and a 'second mob' that arrived by freight train; no one is named and the crowds' race is not stated.
The two men were later taken to Troy for safe keeping; no report of a trial or of their later fate was found.

sources.note: Missouri state-news item 'Saved Lives of Two Negroes': Constable George D. May, Sheriff Lindsey and his family turn back two mobs; prisoners moved to Bowling Green jail, then Troy.
quotes: A large crowd gathered to hang the culprits, but May hustled them away right under the eyes of the would-be lynchers before they had time to organize.
The sheriff, his wife and two daughters, each armed with pistols, convinced the angry men that an advance meant death and after considerable mutterings they dispersed.
